text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: the outdoor condensing unit is running with severely reduced heat-rejection capacity because the condenser coil is loaded with dust/debris while ambient is 92°F, driving discharge pressure and discharge line temperature high enough to trip the high-pressure/thermal protection circuit that Daikin's controller logs and displays as CH21 on the SkyAir wired remote (BRC-series controller). This protection-driven shutdown is what is producing the observed compressor short-cycling, and the reported "noisy expansion valve" is consistent with flash gas or erratic refrigerant flow hunting through the TXV as the system swings between normal operation and high-pressure lockout.
- Code meaning: Daikin light-commercial split "CH" check codes are self-diagnostic fault flags reported through the remote controller rather than a blinking LED count; on SkyAir/Sky-Air FBQ, FXAQ, and RZQ outdoor unit families, codes in the low-20s range are most commonly tied to compressor protection, discharge thermistor abnormality, or high-pressure switch actuation logic — all of which fit a dirty-coil, high-ambient, high-head-pressure event far better than a control-board or communication fault would.
- Component analysis: the 5°F supply-to-return split (normal SkyAir delta-T at these ambient conditions should be 16–22°F) indicates the evaporator is starved of properly conditioned refrigerant, which is exactly what happens when the compressor cycles off on protection before it can pull the system into a stable low-side/high-side balance; the noisy TXV further suggests the valve is seeing intermittent flash gas rather than a pure liquid feed, a downstream symptom of the high head-pressure condition rather than a primary valve failure.
- Age/mileage considerations: at roughly five to six years in service, this SkyAir unit is within normal working life for its compressor and TXV, but it is squarely in the window where condenser coils accumulate enough fin-face dust and cottonwood/debris loading to measurably restrict airflow if annual coil cleaning has been skipped — the recently replaced indoor filter tells you someone is maintaining the indoor side but likely has not addressed the outdoor coil, which matches the technician's own note that the coil is visibly dusty.
- Confidence: 74%. This is below the 80% threshold because the exact CH21 definition cannot be confirmed without the outdoor unit model/serial number (recorded as N/A) — Daikin's CH/check code tables differ between SkyAir generations (R-410A single-phase vs. three-phase commercial models), so the code must be cross-referenced against the specific outdoor unit nameplate before any repair is finalized.
  - Data Needed:
  - Full outdoor unit model and serial number (e.g., RZQ, RXTQ, or similar SkyAir designation) so the correct CH-code table and service manual section can be pulled.
  - Photograph of the wired remote controller (BRC1E/BRC1H) screen showing the exact code sequence and any accompanying inspection code sub-digits.
  - Manifold gauge readings (suction and discharge pressure) taken at the service ports with ambient at or near 92°F, along with measured superheat and subcooling.
  - Compressor amperage draw compared to the nameplate RLA/LRA, and a clamp-meter reading at the contactor.
  - Photos of the condenser coil fin face before and after cleaning, and outdoor fan CFM/static readings if available.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Refrigerant undercharge or leak (moderate-high likelihood): a system low on charge produces low suction pressure, low subcooling, a hissing/noisy TXV from flash gas, and poor delta-T almost identical to what is described here; it is ranked below the dirty-coil theory only because the technician specifically flagged the dusty outdoor coil as an observed condition, but a leak must still be checked with an electronic leak detector before assuming coil cleaning alone will fix it.
- TXV mechanical failure (moderate likelihood): a sticking or eroded valve seat, a lost charge in the power head, or a bulb that has lost contact with the suction line can cause the exact hunting/noise and poor cooling described; this is ranked below airflow/charge issues because TXV bulbs commonly lose strap contact from vibration or improper insulation, which is a low-cost fix worth ruling out before condemning the valve outright.
- Compressor internal wear or valve leakage (lower likelihood): an aging scroll or rotary compressor with worn internal reeds can short-cycle on low capacity and generate abnormal noise, but this would typically show high suction pressure with a lower-than-expected compression ratio rather than the high-head-pressure signature suggested by a dusty coil and 92°F ambient; amperage draw testing will confirm or rule this out.
- Failed or misadjusted anti-short-cycle timer/control board (low likelihood): SkyAir outdoor boards include a compressor protection delay (typically 3 minutes minimum off-time); if this timer relay has degraded, the unit could cycle rapidly independent of pressure conditions, but this would not explain the reported 5°F delta-T or the noisy TXV, so it is ranked last.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Pull the exact CH21 sub-code from the BRC wired controller's diagnostic menu and cross-reference it against the Daikin SkyAir outdoor unit's service manual code table for that specific model — this takes under 30 minutes and should cost no more than a standard $95–$150 diagnostic service call.
- Attach manifold gauges to the service ports and record suction/discharge pressure, superheat, and subcooling with the unit running at 92°F ambient; expect saturated discharge pressure corresponding to roughly 120–130°F condensing temperature on a clean R-410A coil at this ambient — readings well above that point straight to the airflow restriction. Budget roughly $120–$200 for this gauge-and-log procedure if billed separately from the service call.
- Clean the condenser coil (chemical coil cleaner and low-pressure rinse, not a pressure washer directly on the fins) and re-test pressures and delta-T under the same load conditions; a return to normal 16–22°F split after cleaning strongly confirms the airflow-restriction diagnosis. Expect $150–$300 for a proper coil cleaning on a light-commercial split condenser.
- Clamp-meter the compressor run winding amperage against the nameplate RLA and inrush against LRA, and megohm-test the compressor windings to ground if short-cycling continues after the coil is clean — this isolates a failing compressor from a pressure-protection nuisance trip. Typical shop charge for this electrical verification is $60–$100.
- Check TXV bulb strap tightness/insulation and superheat response by warming and cooling the bulb by hand while watching suction pressure react; a sluggish or non-responsive valve after the coil is clean and charge is confirmed correct condemns the TXV itself, avoiding an unnecessary valve replacement.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- "Can you show me the exact CH21 sub-code and where it's defined in the Daikin service manual for this specific outdoor unit model?" — a competent tech should pull up the manual page, not just say "it's a general fault."
- "What were your measured suction and discharge pressures, and calculated superheat/subcooling, before you touched anything?" — no logged numbers means no real diagnosis was performed.
- "Did you clean the coil and re-test before quoting any refrigerant or TXV work?" — if they went straight to recharging or replacing the valve without cleaning the dirty coil first, that is a shortcut, not a diagnosis.
- "What was the compressor's amp draw compared to the nameplate RLA/LRA?" — this number should be on their paperwork; vague answers signal no electrical testing was done.
- "If you're recommending a TXV replacement, what specifically confirmed the valve itself is bad rather than the dirty coil or a charge issue?" — listen for bulb-response testing or superheat data, not just "it sounds bad."

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: "I've done some research on Daikin SkyAir check codes and I'd like to understand what CH21 is telling us on this unit before we approve any repair."
- Phrasing: keep it curious, not accusatory — "Could you walk me through what your pressure readings showed compared to what's normal at this ambient temperature?"
- Example dialogue: "I noticed the outdoor coil was dusty — did cleaning it change your pressure readings at all? I'm just trying to understand the sequence of what you tested."
- Body language: stay relaxed, take notes on a clipboard or phone, and treat this like a facilities-manager review rather than a confrontation — this signals you expect documentation, not that you distrust the technician personally.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say, "I'm not questioning your ability — I just need to document the testing for our maintenance records before I authorize repair costs."
- Exit strategy: "I'd like a written summary of your pressure readings and the coil-cleaning result before we move forward — can you email that over today?"
- Never say: "My AI report says..." or "I got a second opinion online." Always say: "I've done some research and want to understand..."

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Condenser coil cleaning: $150–$300 depending on access and degree of fouling; this should always be step one given the technician's own observation of a dusty coil.
- Refrigerant charge correction (if confirmed low): R-410A typically runs $50–$120 per pound installed at current market rates, and a light-commercial SkyAir split usually holds 6–12 lbs depending on line length, so a partial top-off after a confirmed small leak might run $150–$400 including leak repair labor.
- TXV replacement (only if independently confirmed faulty): OEM Daikin TXV assemblies for SkyAir outdoor units typically run $150–$350 in parts, with 2–3 hours of labor for recovery, replacement, evacuation, and recharge at $130–$180/hr, putting a full valve job at roughly $600–$1,050.
- Compressor amp-draw/electrical diagnostic and full pressure workup: $150–$250 combined labor.
- Fair total for coil cleaning plus full diagnostic verification (before any parts are condemned): $300–$550. If the shop is quoting a full refrigerant recharge and TXV replacement bundled together before cleaning the coil and re-testing, that is a strong overcharge indicator.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts cannon indicator: a quote that bundles a TXV replacement, a full recharge, AND a compressor "just in case" without a documented pressure/amperage workup is replacing components to find the fault at your expense.
- Diagnostic shortcut: if the technician read the CH21 code, glanced at the dusty coil, and jumped straight to a parts quote without gauging the system under load at 92°F ambient, no real verification occurred.
- Price gouging red flag: refrigerant billed above roughly $150/lb installed, or a "diagnostic fee" charged in addition to a flat-rate coil cleaning that was never actually itemized or shown to you.
- Red flag response pattern: vague answers like "it's probably low on freon" or "these units just get noisy" without any superheat/subcooling numbers to back up the claim.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: outdoor coil cleaning and a full pressure/superheat/subcooling workup performed at 92°F ambient — this is the lowest-cost, highest-value first step and matches the shop's own observation of a dusty coil.
- Reject outright: any TXV replacement or full refrigerant recharge quoted before the coil has been cleaned and re-tested under load.
- Get a second opinion: if short-cycling and the CH21 code persist after a documented coil cleaning and confirmed correct refrigerant charge, and the shop still cannot show you compressor amp-draw data, take the pressure logs to another Daikin-authorized dealer before authorizing compressor or major electrical work.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: a SkyAir split system rejects heat at the outdoor coil by pushing ambient air across finned tubing carrying hot, high-pressure refrigerant gas; when that coil is dust-caked, airflow drops, the refrigerant cannot condense efficiently, and both discharge pressure and discharge line temperature climb until the protection board shuts the compressor down to prevent damage — this is precisely the mechanism behind a CH-series protection code paired with short-cycling.
- Failure mechanism: high head pressure forces the TXV to work against an abnormal pressure differential, which can cause it to hunt, whistle, or hiss as it struggles to meter liquid refrigerant properly; over time, repeated high-pressure cycling stresses compressor motor windings and can shorten compressor life even if the coil issue is eventually resolved.
- Prevention: schedule outdoor coil cleaning at least twice a year for units operating in dusty environments or near landscaping debris, and have supply/return delta-T and head pressure logged during each seasonal PM visit so a developing airflow restriction is caught before it triggers a protection lockout in peak summer heat.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Because the exact outdoor unit model is not yet confirmed, the specific Daikin TXV part number cannot be finalized here — once the model/serial is provided, the correct OEM TXV kit number can be pulled from Daikin's parts catalog for that SkyAir outdoor unit family.
- OEM is critical for the TXV specifically because Daikin's factory-matched valves are calibrated to the exact refrigerant charge and metering characteristics of that compressor/coil combination; a generic aftermarket TXV can cause chronic hunting, nuisance high-pressure trips, or poor superheat control even after a coil cleaning fixes the airflow problem.
- Pricing sources: request a written parts quote referencing the Daikin part number from an authorized Daikin distributor or the servicing contractor's parts counter, and compare it against at least one independent Daikin parts supplier before authorizing any TXV replacement.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Ask for the coil-cleaning and re-test to be billed and completed first, separate from any parts replacement, so you are not paying for parts before confirming they are actually needed.
- Request that any recharge be billed by the pound with the amount logged against the nameplate charge for the unit, and question any recharge quote that doesn't reference a specific measured shortfall.
- Walk-away point: if the shop insists on a bundled TXV-plus-recharge repair "or no warranty" without first cleaning the coil and showing you before/after pressure readings, that is leverage to seek a second Daikin-authorized servicer.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: condenser coil airflow restriction from dust loading, compounded by 92°F ambient, driving high head pressure and a CH21 protection trip — 60% confidence, based directly on the technician's own observation of a dusty coil combined with short-cycling and poor delta-T.
- Secondary cause: refrigerant undercharge or slow leak producing low subcooling and TXV noise — 25% confidence; plausible and must be ruled out with gauge readings, since undercharge symptoms overlap heavily with airflow restriction symptoms.
- Tertiary cause: TXV mechanical failure (stuck valve, lost bulb charge, or eroded seat) independent of the coil condition — 15% confidence; possible given the reported valve noise, but less likely to be the sole cause of a system-wide 5°F delta-T without an accompanying pressure abnormality.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate: have the outdoor coil professionally cleaned and the system re-tested for delta-T, pressures, superheat, and subcooling before any refrigerant or TXV work is authorized, especially since the unit is likely working hard through continued 90°F-plus days.
- Future maintenance: place this SkyAir unit on a twice-yearly coil-cleaning and pressure-logging schedule, and keep a written log of delta-T readings each visit so any gradual airflow decline is caught before it trips protection codes again.
- Warning signs to monitor: repeated CH21 codes after a confirmed clean coil and correct charge, any burning electrical smell near the outdoor unit's contactor/capacitor, or compressor amperage trending upward over successive visits — any of these warrants immediate professional attention rather than a wait-and-see approach.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Daikin SkyAir/light-commercial split service manual and outdoor unit installation manual (model-specific) — request the exact document from the servicing contractor once the outdoor unit model/serial is confirmed; it contains the authoritative CH-code definition table.
- ASHRAE Standard 180 (Standard Practice for Inspection and Maintenance of Commercial HVAC Systems) — supports the coil-cleaning and delta-T logging maintenance interval recommended above for commercial split systems operating in dusty environments.
- HVAC-Talk and RSES technician forum threads on Daikin SkyAir "CH" check codes and high head-pressure short-cycling — independent technician discussions confirming that dirty condenser coils in high-ambient conditions are a leading real-world cause of protection-code trips on this product line; use these as a cross-check, not a substitute for the model-specific service manual.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Provide the outdoor unit's model and serial number to the servicing contractor so the exact CH21 definition can be confirmed against the correct Daikin service manual.
- Authorize a professional condenser coil cleaning plus a full pressure/superheat/subcooling workup at or near 92°F ambient before approving any refrigerant charge or TXV replacement.
- Request written before-and-after readings (pressures and delta-T) from the coil cleaning so you can verify the fix worked before any further parts are authorized.
